original_question: For the classical smoothness classes F_d^k(D_d) on volume-1 domains, explicit lower bounds of the form e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) >= min{1/2, c_k d n^{-k/d}} are known. What are the sharp values or sharper estimates of the constants c_k, and which domains D_d are extremal in the sense that, for given k, d, and n, the integration error e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) is especially small?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Remark 7(1) in the "General Domains" discussion, immediately after the recalled lower bound for F_d^k(D_d); this is the place where Novak asks for better information on the constants c_k and on extremal sets D_d for which e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) is small for fixed k,d,n. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2307.06787))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right target very closely: it names the classical smoothness classes F_d^k(D_d), the explicit lower-bound shape e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) >= min{1/2, c_k d n^{-k/d}}, the normalization λ_d(D_d)=1, and the paper’s two actual concerns here—understanding the constants c_k more precisely and identifying extremal domains D_d with unusually small integration error. That is essentially Remark 7(1). ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))
missing_details: The paper’s class should be defined explicitly: F_d^k(D_d) = {f : D_d -> R | ||D^alpha f||_infinity <= 1 for every multi-index alpha with |alpha| <= k}, where |alpha| = sum_{i=1}^d alpha_i and D^alpha f denotes the corresponding partial derivative. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))

The operator and error notion should be stated: S_d(f) = integral over D_d of f(x) dx, and e(n,F_d) is the minimal deterministic worst-case integration error over all algorithms using n function values. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))

The quantifiers are part of the official statement: for every k in N there exists c_k > 0 such that for all d,n in N and all open domains D_d subset R^d with λ_d(D_d)=1, one has e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) >= min{1/2, c_k d n^{-k/d}}. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))

The paper’s wording is about extremal sets D_d for fixed k,d,n, not just domains that are informally 'especially small-error'; the intended problem is to characterize or at least identify such minimizers or near-minimizers among all volume-one domains. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))

Nearby context adds that this lower bound cannot be improved in order, because cubes admit a comparable upper bound; that is part of why the open question focuses on constants and extremal domains rather than on improving the rate itself. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))

A paper-faithful stand-alone version should also mention the caveat that there is no meaningful explicit uniform upper bound over all domains, since sup over D_d of e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) equals 1 unless boundary conditions such as f=0 on ∂D_d are imposed. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))
refined_question: Let D_d subset R^d be an open domain with λ_d(D_d)=1, and define F_d^k(D_d) = {f : D_d -> R | ||D^alpha f||_infinity <= 1 for all multi-indices alpha with |alpha| <= k}. For the integration operator S_d(f) = integral over D_d of f(x) dx, let e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) denote the minimal deterministic worst-case error among all algorithms using n function values. It is known that for every k in N there exists c_k > 0 such that, for all d,n in N and all such D_d, e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) >= min{1/2, c_k d n^{-k/d}}, and that this order is not improvable because cubes satisfy a comparable upper bound. Determine, as sharply as possible, the constants c_k and characterize the extremal volume-one domains D_d, for fixed k,d,n, for which e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) is minimal or especially small. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))
justification: The draft is targeting Remark 7(1), not the broader open problem in Section 2 and not the neighboring Remark 7(2). The reason is that Novak first recalls the exact general-domain lower bound for F_d^k(D_d), then immediately says that one should know more about the constants c_k and about extremal sets D_d where e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) is small for given k,d,n. Section 1 supplies the definitions of S_d and e(n,F_d) needed to make that question stand alone. Remark 7(2), by contrast, is a different question about whether the asymptotic constant lim_{n->infinity} e(n,F_d^k(D_d)) n^{k/d} is independent of D_d, so it should not replace Remark 7(1). ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/936902995/978-3-031-59762-6))
